Despite being called the monkey-eating eagle, the Philippine eagle primarily hunts flying lemurs and large monitor lizards in the wild.
Cecilia Muñoz-Palma became the first Filipina appointed to the Philippine Supreme Court in 1973 by President Ferdinand Marcos.
The ancient Ifugao woodcarvers create bulul statues, which are believed to guard the rice granaries and ensure abundant harvests.
Before the Spanish arrived, early Filipinos wrote on bamboo and palm leaves using the ancient Baybayin alphabetic writing system.
During the Moriones Festival in Marinduque, participants wear carved wooden masks and Roman soldier costumes to reenact the story of Longinus.
Emilio Aguinaldo officially proclaimed Philippine independence from Spanish colonial rule on June 12, 1898, at his home in Kawit, Cavite.
Filipino pediatrician Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator that uses hot water bottles to keep newborns warm in rural areas.
The Philippine pearl, officially declared as the national gem in 1996, is primarily harvested from the coastal waters of Palawan.
Chieftain Lapu-Lapu and his warriors successfully defeated Ferdinand Magellan in the Battle of Mactan on April 27, 1521.
The traditional Filipino value of bayanihan originated from the literal practice of an entire village carrying a nipa hut to a new location.
Juan Luna’s famous painting Spoliarium measures over four meters tall and seven meters wide, depicting fallen gladiators being dragged away.
